## Management of the Chinese muntjac {#sec-management}

(Rapid) eradication and control usually via shooting, although other techniques have been applied (trapping, netting).

From meeting with Bram:\
In principle, two control methods can be distinguished, hunting from a blind (i.e., the hunter sits in a raised hide or hunting blind waiting for animals to pass by; blind hunting in the following) versus stalk hunting or stalking (i.e., the hunter tries to find the animals by walking around attentively, looking and listening).
In the past, hunters from ANB and the non-profit organization (vereniging zonder winstoogmerk) Jonge Jagers used to blind hunt during the winter.
Nowadays, only the more effective, but also more risky, stalking is practised.

In Flanders, management of Chinese muntjac primarily consists of targeted removal through hunting, often initiated through a rapid response protocol.
Control efforts are carried out by a combination of faunabeheerders from the Agency for Nature and Forest (ANB) and authorized hunters.
When a new sighting is reported, the species identification is verified and—if confirmed—a hunter is mobilized as quickly as possible to attempt removal.
In areas where the species has established, two principal methods have been tried: still hunting (aanzitjacht) and stalking (bersjacht).
Still hunting involves positioning a hunter at a fixed vantage point, typically at dawn or dusk, and waiting for an animal to pass by.
However, this method has proven largely ineffective for muntjac control: due to the species’ small size, crepuscular activity, and preference for dense understory cover, detection and shooting opportunities are rare and require long, unproductive waiting periods.
In contrast, stalking—where hunters actively and quietly move through the habitat in search of animals—is markedly more effective.
This technique increases encounter rates and allows hunters to scan undergrowth more thoroughly, particularly in winter when vegetation is sparse.
As a result, stalking is now considered the preferred method for muntjac removal in Flanders.
Although muntjac has proven difficult to remove entirely, some successes have been recorded.
During the 2022–2023 campaign, three animals were shot.
This was followed by ten animals culled during the 2023–2024 campaign.
An additional three individuals were removed in the interim period between these campaigns, bringing the total number of muntjac removed to sixteen over this two-year period.
Despite this effort, the species continues to persist in several forest fragments northeast of Antwerp, suggesting either incomplete detection or ongoing dispersal from nearby areas.
Continued pressure through stalking, particularly during the winter months, is considered key to further reduce the local population.

Detailed information can be found in Casaer et al., 2015 (see also Baiwy et al.)..\
